senses.definition: A senior person putting their own standing behind a piece of work or a person, and spending it when the thing is contested. It covers both an executive sponsor who owns a programme's outcome and the backing that puts someone's name into a promotion discussion.
senses.caution: The line that matters: a mentor talks to you, a sponsor talks about you. Describing someone as your sponsor when all they have given is advice overstates what you have, and it is embarrassing when the room knows them better than you do. The word also means paid branding, so with a mixed audience say executive sponsor the first time and let the rest run short.
senses.example: The programme has funding and it has sponsorship, so when finance pushed back last week it was not my fight alone.

cues.text: A director asks what the failed initiative was really missing, and the honest answer is that nobody senior owned it once it got hard.
You are advising a colleague who has no shortage of mentors and keeps being passed over, and you want the word for the thing mentoring is not.
Before starting a programme that cuts across three teams, you want one word for the senior commitment you will ask for beyond the budget.
A friend's daughter is trying to break into an industry where advice is easy to come by and an opened door is not.
At a climbing club an experienced member vouches for a newcomer and puts her own standing behind them.

distractors: Genuine agreement from the people who actually have to do the work, to the point where they will argue for it when you are not there.
Advice and guidance given privately to somebody less experienced, on how to read a situation and what to do next. Nothing of the giver's own standing is put at risk by it.

Formal budget authority over a programme: the signature that releases the money and the right to stop releasing it. It is a control written into the finance process rather than anything a person chooses to spend on your behalf, and it stays with the role after the holder moves on.

Responsibility for the day-to-day delivery of a project: the person who runs the plan, chases the dependencies and is asked first when a date starts to slip. The job is to make the thing happen week by week, and it is done on organisation and follow-through rather than on any weight the person carries with the people above the programme.

A named contact who handles escalations once the normal route has failed, so that a stuck item has somewhere to go outside the usual queue. The role is a routing decision the organisation published in advance; it costs the person holding it nothing, and their name on the list carries no opinion about whether the thing being escalated deserves to succeed.
